propositions.text: The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness has applied to find that the refugee protection of the respondent has ceased under s.108(2) of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (the "applicant") has applied to the Immigration and Refugee Board to find that the refugee protection of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "respondent") has ceased, pursuant to s.108(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister has applied to the Immigration and Refugee Board to find the respondent's refugee protection ceased under s.108(2) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The Applicant alleges the Respondent voluntarily reavailed of protection of their country under s.108(1)(a) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicant alleges that the Respondent's situation is described in s.108(1)(a) of the Act, i.e. a person who has "voluntarily reavailed themself of the protection of their country of nationality."

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges the Respondent voluntarily reavailed of their country's protection under s.108(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Respondent is a Honduran citizen who came to Canada in 2014 and had a refugee claim accepted in 2005.
propositions.quote: the Respondent, a citizen of Honduras, came to Canada in September 2014 and made a refugee claim against Honduras that was accepted by a member of the Refugee Protection Division on March 21, 2005.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent is a Honduran citizen who came to Canada in 2014 and had a refugee claim accepted in 2005.

propositions.text: The Respondent became a permanent resident of Canada in 2006.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, 2006, the Respondent became a permanent resident of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent became a permanent resident of Canada in 2006.

propositions.text: The Respondent applied for and received a Honduran passport valid from 2009 to 2014.
propositions.quote: The Respondent applied for and received a Honduran passport, valid from XXXX, 2009 to XXXX, 2014.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent applied for and received a Honduran passport valid 2009-2014.

propositions.text: The Respondent used the Honduran passport to travel back to Honduras five times between 2007 and 2014.
propositions.quote: He used this passport to travel back to Honduras five times between 2007 and 2014.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent traveled to Honduras five times between 2007 and 2014 using the passport.

propositions.text: On August 28, 2014, the Minister provided an Application for Cessation of Refugee Protection with notice, grounds, and supporting documentation including CBSA interviews.
propositions.quote: On August 28, 2014, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration Canada provided their Application for Cessation of Refugee Protection, consisting of a notice, grounds for the application, and a volume of supporting documentation, including material obtained via CBSA interviews with the Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: On August 28, 2014, the Minister provided an Application for Cessation with notice, grounds, and supporting documents including CBSA interviews.

propositions.text: On November 29, 2017, the RPD scheduled a hearing for February 16, 2018, later rescheduled.
propositions.quote: On November 29, 2017, the Refugee Protection Division provided a notice to the parties that they should appear for a hearing on this matter on February 16, 2018. This matter was subsequently rescheduled.

paragraphs.summary: On November 29, 2017, the RPD scheduled a hearing for February 16, 2018, later rescheduled.

propositions.text: On June 11, 2018, the Respondent disclosed documents for the hearing.
propositions.quote: On June 11, 2018, the Respondent disclosed documents for the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: On June 11, 2018, the Respondent disclosed documents for the hearing.

propositions.text: On June 22, 2018, the parties appeared at a hearing in Vancouver; a second hearing day was scheduled.
propositions.quote: On June 22, 2018, the parties appeared at a hearing in Vancouver, BC. A second hearing day was then scheduled.

paragraphs.summary: On June 22, 2018, parties appeared at a hearing in Vancouver; a second hearing day was scheduled.

propositions.text: On July 16, 2018, the Respondent requested rejection of the application for procedural fairness reasons.
propositions.quote: On July 16, 2018, the Respondent provided written submissions requesting that the application be rejected for reasons of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: On July 16, 2018, the Respondent requested rejection of the application for procedural fairness reasons.

propositions.text: On August 3, 2018, the Applicant provided written submissions responding to the procedural fairness argument.
propositions.quote: On August 3, 2018, the Applicant provided written submissions on the procedural fairness argument.

paragraphs.summary: On August 3, 2018, the Applicant responded in writing to the procedural fairness argument.

propositions.text: On October 3, 2018, the second hearing day completed the evidentiary portion of the matter.
propositions.quote: On October 3, 2018, the second hearing day took place, which completed the evidentiary portion of this matter.

paragraphs.summary: On October 3, 2018, the second hearing day completed the evidentiary portion of the matter.

propositions.text: On October 17, 2018, the Applicant provided written submissions on evidence and re-availment analysis.
propositions.quote: On October 17, 2018, the Applicant provided written submissions regarding the evidence and analysis of re-availment.

paragraphs.summary: On October 17, 2018, the Applicant submitted written arguments on evidence and re-availment analysis.

propositions.text: On October 29, 2018, the Respondent provided written submissions on evidence and re-availment analysis.
propositions.quote: On October 29, 2018, the Respondent provided written submissions on the evidence and analysis of re-availment.

paragraphs.summary: On October 29, 2018, the Respondent submitted written arguments on evidence and re-availment analysis.

propositions.text: On November 9, 2018, the Applicant provided reply submissions.
propositions.quote: On November 9, 2018, the Applicant provided reply submissions.

paragraphs.summary: On November 9, 2018, the Applicant provided reply submissions.

propositions.text: The Applicant's position is summarized from their submissions.
propositions.quote: The Applicant's position is summarized from their submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant's position is summarized from their submissions.

propositions.text: Per UNHCR Handbook, three criteria for re-availment: voluntary act, intention to re-avail, and actual protection obtained.
propositions.quote: The Applicant notes that, per the UNHCR Handbook, there are three criteria for re-availment. The refugee must have: * Acted voluntarily; * Intended by his action to re-avail himself of the protection of the country of nationality; and * Actually obtained such protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant notes UNHCR Handbook's three criteria for re-availment: voluntary act, intention, and actual protection obtained.

propositions.text: Applicant argues no evidence Respondent was instructed to obtain Honduran passport, supporting voluntariness.
propositions.quote: Regarding voluntariness, the Applicant notes that there is no evidence that the Respondent was instructed to obtain a Honduran passport.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues no evidence Respondent was instructed to obtain Honduran passport, supporting voluntariness.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Respondent's passport applications and travel documents show intention to avail of Honduras' protection.
propositions.quote: Regarding intention, the Applicant submits that the Respondent's two applications for Honduran passports and presentation of his documents to government officials (or agents) while travelling indicate that he intended to avail himself of the diplomatic protection of Honduras.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Respondent was not clandestine or secretive while in Honduras.
propositions.quote: The Applicant additionally submits that, while in Honduras, the Respondent was not "clandestine or cloaked in secrecy in any reasonable way."

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits Respondent's passport applications and travel show intention to avail Honduras' protection and not being secretive in Honduras.

propositions.text: Respondent received two passports and multiple entries to countries, amounting to receipt of diplomatic protection
propositions.quote: the Applicant notes that the Respondent did receive two passports and was allowed multiple entries to a number of countries, which amounts to receipt of diplomatic protection.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Respondent received passports and multiple entries, amounting to diplomatic protection.

propositions.text: Conditions of re-availment under s.108(1)(a) have been met
propositions.quote: the Applicant argues that the conditions of re-availment under s.108(1)(a) have been met.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues conditions of re-availment under s.108(1)(a) are met.

propositions.text: Summarizes Respondent's position from their submissions
propositions.quote: The Respondent's position is summarized from their submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Court summarizes Respondent's position from submissions.

propositions.text: Respondent seeks dismissal of application and advances two arguments
propositions.quote: The Respondent seeks to have the application dismissed. The Respondent advances two arguments.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent seeks dismissal and advances two arguments.

propositions.text: Issue of re-availment arose from abuse of process
propositions.quote: First, the Respondent submits that the issue of re-availment arose from an abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues re-availment issue arose from abuse of process.

propositions.text: Respondent was examined by CBSA Officer returning to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2014
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that, while returning to Canada through Vancouver International Airport on XXXX XXXX, 2014, the Respondent was examined by a CBSA Officer.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent notes examination by CBSA Officer upon return to Canada in 2014.

propositions.text: CBSA Officer had duty to determine if Respondent was valid permanent resident under s.19(2) of the Act
propositions.quote: The Respondent acknowledges that the CBSA Officer had a duty to determine whether the Respondent was a valid permanent resident for the purpose of allowing him to enter Canada per s.19(2) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent acknowledges CBSA Officer's duty to determine permanent resident status under s.19(2).

propositions.text: CBSA Officer asked additional questions about refugee status, returns to Honduras, and fears
propositions.quote: The CBSA Officer went on to ask additional questions, regarding the Respondent's refugee status, returns to Honduras, and his fears.

paragraphs.summary: CBSA Officer asked additional questions about refugee status and returns to Honduras.

propositions.text: CBSA Officer should have informed Respondent of no obligation to answer and right to counsel before extra questioning
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the CBSA Officer ought to have informed the Respondent that he was under no obligation to answer these additional questions, and that he had a right to counsel being present, before examining him on matters which go beyond his statutory authority.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues CBSA Officer failed to inform him of rights before extra questioning.

propositions.text: CBSA Hearings Advisor interviewed Respondent, collected passport copy, told no obligation to answer but not right to counsel
propositions.quote: The CBSA Officer's examination led to a follow-up interview of the Respondent by a CBSA Hearings Advisor, who collected more information and took a copy of the Respondent's passport. The Hearings Advisor did tell the Respondent that he was under no obligation to answer the questions, but failed to advise him of a right to counsel.

paragraphs.summary: CBSA Hearings Advisor interviewed Respondent, told no obligation to answer but not right to counsel.

propositions.text: s.167 of the Act confers right to counsel at proceedings including pre-hearing evidence-gathering interviews
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that s.167 of the Act confers a right to counsel at "proceedings before any Division of the Board and the Minister," and that, per the Federal Court of Appeal,2 such proceedings include pre-hearing evidence-gathering interviews.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent notes s.167 grants right to counsel including pre-hearing interviews.

propositions.text: Panel should exclude evidence obtained in violation of natural justice, leaving Applicant without evidentiary foundation
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the Panel has the authority and obligation to exclude the evidence adduced in violation of natural justice. Excluding the improperly obtained statements and documents collected by the CBSA Officer and Hearings Advisor would leave the Applicant without an evidentiary foundation for its application.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Panel must exclude evidence obtained violating natural justice, undermining Applicant's case.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to prove Respondent voluntarily re-availed himself of Honduras protection
propositions.quote: The second argument of the Respondent is that the Applicant failed to meet its onus to establish that the Respondent voluntarily re-availed himself of the protection of Honduras.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Applicant failed to prove voluntary re-availment of Honduras protection.

propositions.text: Respondent does not dispute Applicant's travel dates, locations, or use of Honduran documents
propositions.quote: The Respondent does not dispute the Applicant's accounting of his travel dates and locations, or the use of Honduran documents.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent does not dispute travel dates, locations, or use of Honduran documents.

propositions.text: Primary issue is assessing motivation to obtain passport and return to Honduras
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the primary issue before the Panel is to assess the motivation to obtain a passport and return to Honduras.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits primary issue is motivation to obtain passport and return to Honduras.

propositions.text: Respondent was isolated from family due to protection status in Canada, placing him in difficult position
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that he was effectively isolated from his family because of his protection status in Canada. This isolation placed him in a difficult position.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent notes isolation from family due to protection status placed him in difficult position.

propositions.text: Respondent took calculated risk obtaining Honduran documents to see son and attend ill parents
propositions.quote: According to his credible testimony, the Respondent took a calculated risk in obtaining Honduran documents for the purpose of seeing his son and to attend to his aging parents who were in ill health.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent took calculated risk obtaining documents to see son and ill parents.

propositions.text: Respondent did not return to Honduras voluntarily but was compelled by love and circumstances
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the Respondent submits, he did not return to Honduras of his own free will, but was "compelled by his love, affection, and circumstances." His intent to request a passport was not, in that sense, truly voluntary.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits return to Honduras was compelled, not voluntary.

propositions.text: Distinction exists between contacting authorities for protection and for other purposes
propositions.quote: Regarding protection, the Respondent submits that a distinction must be made between contacting authorities to obtain protection, and contacting authorities for any other purpose.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues distinction between contacting authorities for protection and other purposes.

propositions.text: Acquiring passport is neutral factor; Respondent never filed refugee claim based on fear of authorities but fears non-state agents
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that "acquiring a passport is not a determining but a neutral factor in this Application," in that the Respondent never filed a refugee claim on the basis of a fear of the authorities. Rather, the Respondent feared, and continues to fear, non-state agents of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues acquiring passport is neutral; fear is of non-state agents, not authorities.

propositions.text: Respondent did not seek protection during returns to Honduras, kept low profile, avoided contacts, used agents for documents, subjective fear persisted
propositions.quote: The Respondent did not seek the protection of the authorities in his returns to Honduras. He kept a low profile during his returns, staying at home and other safe areas, avoiding friends and neighbours, and using agents to assist with obtaining documentation. His subjective fear persisted.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent did not seek protection during returns to Honduras, kept a low profile, and his subjective fear persisted, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The Applicant's application is rejected
propositions.quote: The application of the Applicant is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Applicant's application.

propositions.text: Applicant provided ample notice to Respondent of application and supporting facts
propositions.quote: I find that the Applicant provided ample notice to the Respondent of its application and supporting facts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant gave ample notice to the Respondent of the application and facts.

propositions.text: Both parties had sufficient opportunity to argue points at hearing and in writing
propositions.quote: I also find that both parties had sufficient opportunity to argue their respective points, at the hearing and through written submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds both parties had sufficient opportunity to argue their points at hearing and in writing.

propositions.text: Analysis begins with Respondent's procedural fairness argument about deleting unfairly obtained material
propositions.quote: As stated to the parties during the hearing, the analysis commences with the Respondent's procedural fairness argument that unfairly obtained material should be deleted, leaving no evidentiary basis for a finding of cessation.

paragraphs.summary: The court begins analysis with Respondent's argument that unfairly obtained material should be deleted.

propositions.text: Objections supported by case law that evidence-gathering interviews are hearings requiring notice of right to counsel
propositions.quote: The Respondent's objections are clearly argued and supported by case law which confirms that evidence-gathering interviews are "hearings" that require the person considered to be notified of a right to counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues with case law that evidence-gathering interviews are hearings requiring notice of right to counsel.

propositions.text: Case cited by Respondent was decided after 2014 airport interview, but retroactivity argument does not invalidate current law
propositions.quote: I acknowledge the Applicant's argument that the case cited by the Respondent was determined after the airport interview in 2014. However, a retroactivity/retrospectivity argument does not invalidate the need to conduct official interactions in a way that conforms to the law as it is understood today.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the case cited was decided after 2014 interview, but retroactivity does not invalidate current legal standards.

propositions.text: Right to counsel for hearings exists and was not made clear to Respondent when obtaining information
propositions.quote: Based on the evidence and law before this Panel, the right to counsel for hearings exists, and that right was not made clear to the Respondent when obtaining his information.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the right to counsel exists and was not made clear to the Respondent during information gathering.

propositions.text: Case law and natural justice require disregarding material from non-jurisdictional interviews without notice of right to counsel
propositions.quote: I find that the case law and natural justice considerations oblige the Panel to disregard material obtained as a result of non-jurisdictional interviews done without the benefit of notice of right of counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds that material from interviews without notice of right to counsel must be disregarded.

propositions.text: RPD decision VB4-01404 excluded evidence obtained unfairly; this reasoning is adopted though not binding
propositions.quote: This is the approach taken by the RPD in a different cessation application, VB4-01404.3 This decision is not binding on other RPD Panels, but I adopt its reasoning with respect to the exclusion of evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court adopts reasoning from RPD decision VB4-01404 to exclude unfairly obtained evidence, though not binding.

propositions.text: Questions and answers from CBSA Officer and Hearings Advisor are not considered
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I have not considered the questions and answers from the CBSA Officer4 and Hearings Advisor.5

paragraphs.summary: The court excludes questions and answers from CBSA Officer and Hearings Advisor from consideration.

propositions.text: Evidence not excluded includes Respondent's Declaration Card, permanent resident card, passport, and boarding pass
propositions.quote: Evidence that has not been excluded because of fairness reasons include the Respondent's Declaration Card stating that his citizenship is "Residents,"6 and his permanent resident card, passport, and boarding pass.7

paragraphs.summary: The court finds certain identity and travel documents are admissible evidence.

propositions.text: These materials reasonably show Respondent's identity and eligibility to return to Canada
propositions.quote: I find that the above materials would reasonably have been provided by the Respondent in order to show who he is, and that he is a person eligible to return to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds these documents reasonably show the Respondent's identity and eligibility to return to Canada.

propositions.text: Respondent argues exclusion leaves Applicant with no basis for cessation request
propositions.quote: To the argument of the Respondent that this leaves the Applicant with nothing upon which to advance its cessation request, the Applicant replies that returning to Canada on a Honduran passport after receiving Convention Refugee status is sufficient to make a prima facie case for cessation of his status.

propositions.text: Applicant replies returning on Honduran passport after refugee status suffices for prima facie cessation case
propositions.quote: To the argument of the Respondent that this leaves the Applicant with nothing upon which to advance its cessation request, the Applicant replies that returning to Canada on a Honduran passport after receiving Convention Refugee status is sufficient to make a prima facie case for cessation of his status.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues exclusion leaves no basis for cessation; the Applicant replies returning on Honduran passport suffices for prima facie cessation.

propositions.text: Applicant's case would be clear and strong with documents plus knowledge Respondent was refugee claimant
propositions.quote: I agree that the Applicant's case would have been clear, and perhaps strong, with these stated documents in hand, plus the knowledge that the Respondent had been a refugee claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the Applicant's case would be strong with documents and knowledge of Respondent's refugee claimant status.

propositions.text: Crucial question: how did Applicant know Respondent was a Convention Refugee apart from improperly obtained admission?
propositions.quote: The crucial question then arises: how did the Applicant come to know that the Respondent was a Convention Refugee, apart from the improperly-obtained admission that he is a former refugee claimant who has no fear of Honduras?

paragraphs.summary: The court raises the issue of how the Applicant knew the Respondent was a Convention Refugee apart from improperly obtained admission.

propositions.text: No clear answer in the evidence about how Applicant knew Respondent's refugee status
propositions.quote: I do not see a clear answer in the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no clear evidence explaining how the Applicant knew the Respondent's refugee status.

propositions.text: Speculation that refugee status is available via database to CBSA officers at points of entry
propositions.quote: One could speculate. It's quite possible that refugee determination is a status that is available via database to CBSA officers who work at points of entry, and that such information is automatically flagged, or that there is a policy to routinely seek immigration history when determining eligibility to enter Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court speculates refugee status may be accessible via database to CBSA officers at points of entry.

propositions.text: Reasonable for CBSA officers to check refugee status when examining eligibility to enter Canada
propositions.quote: To go even further, I suggest it is entirely reasonable for CBSA officers to make these checks when examining people for eligibility to enter. Refugee status being a highly limited exception to the immigration procedures of signatory nations, Canada has every right to gather information for cessation and vacation applications in order to remove those who do not need protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court suggests it is reasonable for CBSA officers to check refugee status when examining eligibility to enter Canada.

propositions.text: Evidence does not show CBSA officer saw Respondent's refugee status before improper questioning
propositions.quote: However, the evidence does not tell me that the CBSA officer, prior to improperly questioning the Respondent, actually spotted his refugee determination on the computer system.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence that the CBSA officer saw the Respondent's refugee status before improper questioning.

propositions.text: Cessation of refugee status should not depend on technically possible but common sense actions not done.
propositions.quote: I do not believe that such a consequential matter as cessation of a person's refugee status should hinge on things that are technically possible, and out of simple common sense ought to have been done.

propositions.text: Panel cannot approve cessation application without sufficient admissible evidence.
propositions.quote: Where there is insufficient admissible evidence, the Panel cannot approve the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds cessation should not hinge on technicalities and requires sufficient admissible evidence to approve cessation.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to provide sufficient admissible evidence that CBSA Officer knew returnee was a past refugee recipient at airport.
propositions.quote: I find that the Applicant has not provided sufficient admissible evidence that the CBSA Officer knew, at the airport, that the returnee was a past recipient of refugee protection, thereby justifying further investigation and ultimately this application for cessation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant did not provide enough admissible evidence that CBSA knew the returnee's refugee status at the airport.

propositions.text: Applicant did not meet onus to show Respondent voluntarily re-availed protection of nationality country.
propositions.quote: I find that the Applicant has not met its onus to show that the Respondent, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a person who has voluntarily re-availed himself of the protection of his country of nationality.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant failed to prove the respondent voluntarily re-availed protection of his country.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The application is therefore dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application.
